To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the material law is the most crucial factor for understanding the longitudinal response of type-II slab geometry superconductors and that the flux cutting threshold is a key ingredient for understanding the electrodynamic response of superconductors in the longitudinal geometry.

the longitudinal critical state in type-II superconducting slabs can be described in terms of anisotropic material laws that account for the flux cutting mechanism, which is responsible for the occurrence of negative current density patterns and a maximal transport current flow at the sample center.

(i) the material law is the most important parameter to be considered in order to understand the longitudinal transport response of type-II slabs; (ii) the flux cutting threshold is the most important material parameter to be measured; and (iii) the flux cutting is the key mechanism to be considered in the longitudinal transport response, as it induces an anisotropic distribution of the transport current, which is strongly correlated to the occurrence of paramagnetic peak effects.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the study of material laws in the context of the critical state model, with the aim of providing a theoretical framework to understand and predict the electromagnetic behavior of type-II superconductor samples in the presence of a longitudinal magnetic field.
the electromagnetic response of a superconducting slab under longitudinal transport current flow.
a systematic analysis of the longitudinal transport problem in a superconducting slab, which is of interest for the development of a new generation of superconducting magnets.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the macroscopic material laws are able to account for the underlying physics of type-II superconductor in longitudinal geometry.
the longitudinal transport measurements provide a unique opportunity for the experimental characterization of the macroscopic flux creep and depinning laws in the superconducting state.

a proper understanding of flux cutting and related depinning phenomena in type-II superconducting materials is mandatory to correctly describe the electromagnetic response of the critical state in longitudinal geometry.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the longitudinal transport current density is the key ingredient to understand the electromagnetic behavior of type-II superconductor slabs in a wide range of applied magnetic fields.
the longitudinal transport problem in type-II superconducting samples can be properly understood by considering the underlying mechanisms of the magnetically-induced internal anisotropies.
the longitudinal transport problem is a very promising experimental setup to characterize the microscopic mechanisms that govern the flux cutting process and the flux depinning threshold.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the longitudinal transport problem in type-II superconducting slabs should be considered as a fundamental benchmark for the experimental validation of theoretical approaches to the critical state problem in the presence of magnetic field modulation.
the longitudinal geometry is an excellent tool to investigate the microscopic mechanisms of the critical state problem in type-II superconducting slabs.
, in order to properly describe the electromagnetic response in type-II superconducting samples, the material law should account not only for the flux cutting but also for the depinning mechanism.
